nb|Lesotho|name||en-Lesotho-nb-name-Za6f.etymology_text:
Internationalism, based on Sotho Lesotho (“land of the Basotho (Sotho people)”). The immediate transmission route into Norwegian is unknown.
The Sotho name belongs to a characteristic noun-class pattern based on Sotho: Mosotho (“a Sotho person”), Basotho (“Sotho people”), Sesotho (“Sotho language”) and Lesotho (“land of the Basotho”).
Parallel international adaptations include Norwegian Nynorsk Lesotho, Afrikaans Lesotho, Swedish Lesotho, German Lesotho, Dutch Lesotho and English Lesotho.

nb|Jupiter|name|1|en-Jupiter-nb-name-W~X.etymology_text:
Internationalism, based on Latin Iuppiter (“Jupiter, the chief Roman god”), also Iūpiter. The Latin nominative continues an ancient vocative expression combining the name of the sky god with pater (“father”), essentially “Father Jove”; compare the oblique stem Iov-, seen in the genitive Iovis.
The name continues Proto-Italic *djous patēr (“sky father”), from *djous (“day, sky”) + *patēr (“father”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *dyḗws (“sky; sky god”) and *ph₂tḗr (“father”). The first element belongs to the Proto-Indo-European root *dyew- (“to be bright; day sky”).
The astronomical sense is transferred from the name of the deity. In the Greco-Roman planetary naming tradition, the planet came to bear the name of Jupiter, the supreme Roman god.
Close cognates of the ancient divine title include Umbrian 𐌉𐌖𐌐𐌀𐌕𐌄𐌓 (iupater, “Jupiter”), Sanskrit द्यौष्पितृ (dyauṣpitṛ, “Sky Father”) and Ancient Greek Ζεῦ πάτερ (Zeû páter, “O father Zeus”). The first element also has cognates Hittite 𒅆𒄿𒌑𒍑, Old Armenian տիւ (tiw), Messapic ζισ (zis) and Lithuanian dievas (“god”).

Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *h₁én
Proto-Germanic *in
Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰengʰ-der.
Proto-Germanic *ganganąder.?
Proto-Germanic *gagin
Proto-Germanic *in gagin
Proto-West Germanic *in gagin
Old English onġēander.
Middle English ayenes
English against
Formed from Middle English ayenes, agenes, againes (“in opposition to”), a southern variant of agen, or directly from again, either way with adverbial genitive singular ending -es; the parasitic -t was added circa 1350, probably by confusion with the superlative ending -est. By surface analysis, again + -st (excrescent ending).
Cognate with Saterland Frisian juun (“against”), West Frisian tsjin (“against”), Dutch tegen (“against”), German Low German gegen (“against”), German gegen (“against”), Icelandic gegn (“against”).
